headline: Stellwagen Basin mud in 100 feet: haddock stacked tight, cod thin, bluefin still working the bait balls
subhead: The gravel gave up fewer cod than August but the mud never let up on haddock, and the tuna are still finding mackerel on the edges.
body_markdown:
Ninety to one-hundred-ten feet of water on the Stellwagen Basin mud, that's where the week lived. Haddock have been stacked on the bottom third of the water column there since the tide swings started running harder with the moon building toward new phase on the 10th, and the jig bite has stayed dependable even when the wind's had an opinion about it. Cod, on the other hand, thinned out on the gravel edges this week — not gone, but scattered enough that you have to work for a limit instead of filling the box on the first drift.

That's the trade-off in early September on this Bank. The gravel humps along Stellwagen Edge, the classic 100-to-140-foot stuff where cod like to sit tight to the rougher bottom, produced fish but in shorter windows — best on the top of the tide change, dead in the middle of a slack. Boats working diamond jigs tipped with a sliver of squid, or straight bait rigs with clam and herring chunks, did fine when they hit the window right. Miss it by even forty-five minutes and it's a lot of reeling for not much. The haddock don't play that game the same way — softer bottom, more consistent metabolism, and they've been willing to eat top-and-bottom rigs with a bit of Berkley Gulp or plain clam belly all day long on the mud sections of the Basin. If you only have room in the fish box for one species this week, the haddock are the better bet.

Offshore, the tuna picture held about where we thought it would. We flagged this last week — said to expect continued mixed action as long as the thermal setup holds — and that's exactly what's played out. The water out toward Tillies Bank and along the edges near Carter Canyon has stayed cooler than what's sitting to the south, which is normal for early September in the Gulf of Maine, and that's kept the pelagic mix centered on bluefin rather than anything warmer-water. Whales have been showing consistently on bait balls out that way, and where the whales are working, the mackerel are getting pinned, and where the mackerel are getting pinned, the bluefin are showing up to finish the job. It's not been an all-day free-for-all — more a matter of finding the right push of bait and being patient enough to sit on it. Boats trolling green machines and spreader bars behind the whale activity have had shots, and the jig-and-drop crowd working live or fresh-dead mackerel under diving birds has connected too, mostly on fish in the 50-to-150-pound class, with the occasional giant mixed in when the bait ball holds together long enough.

Pollock have been a decent consolation prize mixed in with the haddock on the Basin mud, taking the same jigs meant for haddock, and a few hake have shown on the deeper edges toward the Basin's outer lip, mostly at night or in low light on bait rigs fished right on bottom. Nothing to build a trip around, but worth knowing if the haddock slow down and you need something else to show for the day.

Wind's been the bigger factor than temperature this week — the usual early-September pattern of building southwesterlies in the afternoon that flatten out overnight, which is why the morning bite on the gravel has been more reliable than the afternoon one. Tide is doing what tide does this time of year with the moon working toward new phase on the 10th: bigger swings, stronger current on the Basin and Edge both, which pushes bait around and can turn a dead stretch of mud into a hot one in twenty minutes if the current lines up right with a bait push.

Looking at the next several days, the setup favors haddock over cod if you're picking one target — the mud has been the more forgiving bite all week and there's no reason to think that changes before the new moon tide arrives. If the tuna crowd wants a piece of the bluefin action, the smart play is watching for whale activity out toward Tillies Bank and Carter Canyon rather than running blind — where the whales sit, the bait sits, and where the bait sits, the fish show. That pattern has held all week and there's nothing in the water column suggesting it breaks before the bigger tide arrives around the 10th. If the wind stays out of the southwest and builds like it has been, plan morning trips on the gravel for cod and save the afternoon slack for working the Basin mud on haddock. Best case, the bait stays concentrated through the new moon push and the tuna bite tightens up rather than scatters. If a front comes through and stirs things up, expect the cod to scatter further and the tuna to follow the bait wherever it settles next — which this time of year usually means deeper, not shallower.
